relationship: Rescue of the soul and only one
rationale: Both pleas pair the speaker's soul with an additional expression: the only one here and the only life there. Both request rescue using hostile animal imagery, with the dog and sword here distinct from the lions there.

relationship: Seeking the face of Jacob's God
rationale: Both describe seeking the Lord and His face. This source identifies Him as Jacob's God, while the target addresses Abraham's offspring and Jacob's sons and adds continual seeking and remembrance of wonders.

relationship: Truth as a guide toward God
rationale: The source asks to be guided into divine truth; the target asks God to send light and truth and reports that they guided the speaker to His holy dwelling.
The petition to be brought out of expanding heart-afflictions corresponds to the other prayer's assurance that God will bring the soul out of distress in His righteousness.
Both speak of God redeeming Israel: this source names all its afflictions, while the target names all its lawless deeds. The objects of redemption remain distinct.

Both refuse participation in ungodly company. This source names sitting with a council of emptiness and entering with transgressors; Psalm1 distinguishes walking in ungodly counsel, standing in sinners' way and sitting with pestilent men.

The psalm joins washed hands among the innocent with going around the altar; Exodus prescribes hand-and-foot washing when priests approach the altar. The ritual comparison does not identify the psalm's speaker as an Aaronic priest.

The psalm maintains confidence even before an army; Elisha tells his fearful attendant not to fear the encircling force because of the greater protection with them. The narrative illustrates the stance without dating the psalm to that event.

The speaker becomes a reproach to neighbors and a fear to acquaintances, while outside observers flee; the target distinguishes friends and neighbors standing opposite from the nearest standing far away. The comparison preserves these different reactions within nearby relationships.
Both prayers oppose deceitful lips and arrogant speech: one asks that they become speechless, the other that the Lord destroy them. The source specifically names their attacks on the righteous.
Both depict divine protection with dwelling imagery: the source promises shelter in a tent from human strife, while the target joins sojourning in God's dwelling with shelter beneath His wings.
The promise of instruction in the way corresponds to the other prayer's request that God teach His paths and guide in truth. The speaker of this promise is not assigned an identity beyond the verse.
The Lord surveys the earth's inhabitants from His dwelling; the target joins His heavenly throne and holy temple with eyes toward the needy and eyelids examining the sons of men.
